The ai bubble is a stress test for ai technology. Its a huge experiment that will ultimately weed out the unsuccessful companies or the companies that can sustain the cost burn long enough for ai and robots to become truely useful technologies. Most individual companies may never become sustainable businesses. But their research does not necessarily disappear when they fail. Their useful components can be purchased, licensed, open-sourced, absorbed by employees’ next companies, or reconstructed by competitors. 
 
That means the bubble can be viewed as a gigantic, decentralized research program in which private investors pay for parallel experiments and the survivors later collect the best results.

At the cost of millions of lives I don’t think this cycle is worth it. Most useful technologies we rely on today are developed by military or state funding anyways, not companies. iPhone, medical equipment, and so forth. The fix isn't censorship. It's structural: public financing, full disclosure, and rules that keep district races district-controlled.

I think the key difference is that many Korean investors were borrowing extraordinary amounts of money to enter the market, creating unusually high levels of leverage. The U.S. market is much older and more established than the KOSPI (To give you an idea, the U.S. market started in 1792 whereas South Korea officially became a modern nation in 1948). A large share of U.S. investing also occurs through long-term retirement accounts such as 401(k)s and IRAs. Day traders certainly exist, but they represent only a small portion of the overall market compared with institutional investors and long-term retirement savers.

So, while I agree that what's happening in South Korea could have some impact on the U.S. market, I don't believe that impact would be especially severe. It's also worth noting that 17 of the world's 20 largest publicly traded companies by market capitalization are American, while no South Korean company is on that list. The scale of the U.S. economy is also enormous; individual states such as California and New York have economies larger than those of many countries.

One thing I've noticed in markets is that parabolic moves rarely end gently. The steeper and faster the climb, the more violent the eventual correction tends to be. It's similar to a ball dropped from a great height: the greater the height, the greater the impact. Markets often behave in reverse: the more explosive the rise, the more severe the unwind can become. By contrast, a steady, sustainable climb is more likely to be followed by an orderly correction than a sudden collapse.

I think many people who piled into the Korean market underestimated that risk. A market that rises nearly 200% in a year isn't behaving normally, especially when just a couple of dominant companies drive a significant portion of its performance. Concentration can amplify both the gains on the way up and the losses if sentiment reverses.

I don't think the KOSPI drop should be treated as an indicator on AI. 
KOSPI went up by a grand total of 20% from the start of 2011 to the end of 2024. The S&P 500 rose 366% in the same period, and the dow jones rose 268%. 
KOSPI rose quickly for good reason, then all the individual investors got really excited to see KOSPI have significant growth for the first time since 2020 (when it rose 40% compared to pre-covid levels and 60% compared to mid-covid levels over one full year). It peaked at 251% above what it had been 13 months ago (when the growth started). 

If you look at the graph of the S&P 500 or the dow jones, you can easily find periods where the value increased by over 20% in less than a year. KOSPI hadn't done this in 5 years. 
Individual investors, when they see an index rise like this, put money in it. They don't really know what the true value of KOSPI is, just that it's going up and that they could make a lot of money off of it. 
Then, the excitement pushed the value too high, and people who had a rough idea of the true value of KOSPI pulled out. 

KOSPI still has a higher value than it did back in April, and it's still twice as high as its value a year ago (as of the writing of this comment, though this could easily change).

Important topic, but the video overstates parts of it. The Korean market did fall sharply, and leverage made losses worse. However, the 14 million figure means Korean stockholders overall not 14 million people borrowing money or going all-in on Samsung and SK hynix. The ₩3 trillion liquidation claim also needs a clearer source. Warning about leverage is fair, but calling it a national collapse or blaming the U.S. alone is misleading.

full detail:
This is an important topic, but some clarification is needed. The Korean market really did experience a severe correction, and leverage clearly made the losses worse. Goldman Sachs estimated that 1.2 million leveraged accounts received margin calls and around 320,000–360,000 accounts were fully liquidated.
